title: Selecting & Filtering
blurb: Filtering is row semantics made executable: decide what each row means, then keep exactly the rows that mean what you want.

cells.title: A boolean mask is a question asked of every row
cells.body:
Filtering a table starts with a question that has a yes/no answer per row: is this order above 150? In pandas you ask the question against a whole column at once — orders["amount"] > 150 — and get back a Series of True/False values, one per row, aligned to the table by position. Passing that mask back into the frame with orders[mask] keeps exactly the rows that answered True.

The habit to build: translate every filter into a per-row question before touching pandas. If you cannot phrase the rule as something each individual row either satisfies or fails, you are not ready to code it. This is what people mean when they say what each row means decides what the operation does — the row is the unit of meaning, and the mask is its cross-examination.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "amount": [120, 200, 350],
})
mask = orders["amount"] > 150
print(mask.tolist())
print(orders[mask])

cells.title: Combine questions with & and | — and mind the parentheses
cells.body:
Python's and/or ask "is this whole object truthy?" — the wrong question for a column holding a thousand answers. pandas overloads & and | to combine two masks element-wise, and because they bind tighter than comparisons, every comparison needs its own parentheses: (df["a"] > 1) & (df["b"] < 5). For "the value is one of these" reach for .isin([...]) instead of a chain of | — it reads like the intent and scales to any list length.

Filtering also never reorders rows: the survivors keep their original order. That guarantee is what makes "rows in first-appearance order" a promise you can write into a spec and keep without an explicit sort.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

logs = pd.DataFrame({
    "service": ["auth", "billing", "auth", "search"],
    "level": ["warn", "error", "error", "info"],
})
core = logs["service"].isin(["auth", "billing"])
print((core & (logs["level"] == "error")).tolist())
print(logs[core & (logs["level"] == "error")])

cells.title: Order is part of the answer, not a detail
cells.body:
Two tables can hold the same rows and still be different answers, because order is information. When a task says "the best per student", a tie between attempts makes "the best" ambiguous until you state how ties break. The professional move is to make ordering explicit: sort_values with exact keys and directions, plus a stated tie-break.

Sorting a frame by group and value — for example sort_values(["student", "score"], ascending=[True, False]) — turns "rank within group" questions into positional questions: after that sort, the first row of each student is their best attempt, the second row is their second-best. Ranking becomes row arithmetic, and tie rules become sort rules you can point at.

exercise.title: Orders above the line
exercise.statement:
A shop reviews its orders table. Each row is one order with columns order_id (int), customer (str) and amount (float).

Implement big_orders(orders, min_amount) that returns a DataFrame with exactly the columns ["order_id", "amount"] (in that order) containing the orders whose amount is strictly greater than min_amount. Rows keep the original table order (first-appearance order).
constraints: Return a DataFrame with exactly the columns ['order_id', 'amount'] in that order
Keep only rows with amount strictly greater than min_amount (equal does not pass)
Rows appear in the same order as in the input table
If no order passes, return an empty DataFrame that still has the two columns

examples.returns: DataFrame with columns ['order_id', 'amount'] and two rows: the orders of 200 and 350
examples.why: 120 and 90 are not strictly greater than 150, so only two rows survive, in their original order
no amount is above 500, so the result keeps the columns but zero rows

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def big_orders(orders, min_amount):
    """Return the orders with amount strictly greater than min_amount.

    Result is a DataFrame with columns ['order_id', 'amount'],
    rows in the original table order.
    """
    pass
hints: Can you phrase the rule as a per-row question? What does one True/False value in orders['amount'] > min_amount correspond to?
Build the boolean mask from the amount column, then use it to select rows and the two columns you need — loc accepts both at once.
mask = orders['amount'] > min_amount, then return orders.loc[mask, ['order_id', 'amount']]. Filtering preserves the input row order, so no sort is needed.
exercise.reasoning: The whole exercise is one per-row question — is this order's amount strictly above the threshold? — asked of every row at once. The mask is aligned to the frame by position, so orders.loc[mask, cols] keeps exactly the rows whose answer is True. Filtering is guaranteed to preserve first-appearance order, which is why the output needs no explicit sort. Selecting the column list inside the same loc call answers "which rows" and "which columns" in one expression — the two halves of every selection problem, decided together.
exercise.solution:
import pandas as pd

def big_orders(orders, min_amount):
    """Return the orders with amount strictly greater than min_amount."""
    mask = orders["amount"] > min_amount
    return orders.loc[mask, ["order_id", "amount"]]

exercise.title: The shortlist: departments and a salary window
exercise.statement:
HR is building a shortlist from the employees table. Each row is one employee with columns name (str), dept (str), salary (int) and years (int).

Implement shortlist(employees, depts, salary_min, salary_max) returning a DataFrame with exactly the columns ["name", "dept", "salary"] (in that order) with the employees whose dept is one of the values in the list depts and whose salary is between salary_min and salary_max, both ends inclusive. Rows keep the original table order.
constraints: Return a DataFrame with exactly the columns ['name', 'dept', 'salary'] in that order
dept membership is tested against the depts list; an empty list matches nobody
salary_min <= salary <= salary_max, both ends inclusive
Rows appear in the same order as in the input table

examples.returns: DataFrame with columns ['name', 'dept', 'salary'] holding the employees with salary 70 and 90 (eng/ops only)
examples.why: the 55 salary is below the window, 95 is above it, and both ends 60/90 are inclusive so 90 passes
no department is in the empty list, so the dept condition filters out every row

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def shortlist(employees, depts, salary_min, salary_max):
    """Return employees in the given departments whose salary is
    within [salary_min, salary_max] (inclusive).

    Result has columns ['name', 'dept', 'salary'], rows in the
    original table order.
    """
    pass
hints: You have two independent per-row questions — 'is the dept in the list?' and 'is the salary inside the window?'. How do you AND two column-sized lists of answers?
Use .isin(depts) for membership, then combine with the two salary comparisons using & — each comparison wrapped in its own parentheses — and index the frame with the combined mask.
exercise.reasoning: A shortlist is the conjunction of per-row questions: each row must satisfy every condition at once. pandas spells conjunction element-wise with &, and each operand must already be a full column of answers — that is why .isin(depts) beats a hand-rolled loop over departments: it produces one mask for the whole list. Because the final mask has one boolean per row, the surviving rows are exactly those where every question answered True, and they emerge in first-appearance order — the same guarantee as any single-condition filter, now composed.
exercise.solution:
import pandas as pd

def shortlist(employees, depts, salary_min, salary_max):
    """Return employees in the given departments whose salary is
    within [salary_min, salary_max] (inclusive)."""
    mask = (employees["dept"].isin(depts)
            & (employees["salary"] >= salary_min)
            & (employees["salary"] <= salary_max))
    return employees.loc[mask, ["name", "dept", "salary"]]

exercise.title: Second-best attempt, ties included
exercise.statement:
A gaming club records practice attempts. Each row of attempts is one attempt with columns student (str), attempt (int id) and score (int). Students have different numbers of attempts and equal scores happen.

Implement second_best(attempts) returning a DataFrame with exactly the columns ["student", "score"] (in that order): one row per student who has at least two attempts, showing that student's second-highest attempt. The second-highest is defined by sorting that student's attempts by score descending and taking the score in position 2 — so duplicates count as separate attempts: attempts 9, 9, 7 have second-highest 9. Rows are sorted by student ascending (alphabetical). Students with fewer than two attempts do not appear at all.
constraints: One row per student with at least two attempts; students with one attempt never appear
Second-highest = the score in position 2 after sorting that student's attempts by score descending (duplicates count)
Return a DataFrame with exactly the columns ['student', 'score'] in that order

examples.call: second_best(attempts)  # ana scored 7 then 9, bo scored 5 then 3, cy scored 10 once
examples.why: ana sorted descending is 9, 7 so position 2 is 7; bo is 5, 3 so position 2 is 3; cy has only one attempt and is left out
with duplicates counting, dee sorted descending is 9, 9, 7 — the second position holds another 9

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def second_best(attempts):
    """Return each student's second-highest attempt.

    One row per student with at least two attempts, columns
    ['student', 'score'], rows sorted by student ascending.
    Duplicates count as separate attempts.
    """
    pass

tests.label: names out of order in input

hints: If every student's attempts were sorted best-first, 'second-highest' would stop being a comparison. What would it become instead?

Sort the whole frame by student ascending and score descending. Now each student's best attempt is the first row of their block and the second-best is the second row — you need the second row of each block.

ranked = attempts.sort_values(['student', 'score'], ascending=[True, False]); keep = ranked.groupby('student').cumcount() == 1; return ranked.loc[keep, ['student', 'score']]. Students with one attempt never reach cumcount 1.
exercise.reasoning: The reframe that unlocks this: ranking is sorting plus position. Once the frame is sorted by student then score descending, "second-highest" is literally the second row of each student's block — no comparisons, no max-of-the-rest gymnastics. Counting rows within each group (groupby(...).cumcount()) marks positions, and a student with a single attempt never produces a row numbered 1, so the at-least-two rule enforces itself. Note why duplicates must count: the tie rule is defined on attempts, not distinct scores, which is exactly the kind of decision the row semantics force you to make explicit.

exercise.title: Cap the sensor spikes at the 90th percentile
exercise.statement:
An IoT gateway logs delivery times. Each row of readings is one delivery with columns delivery (str id), route (str) and minutes (float). A few deliveries get stuck in traffic and produce spikes that ruin every chart.

Implement cap_outliers(readings) that computes the 90th percentile of the minutes column over all rows with .quantile(0.9) (pandas default interpolation), and returns a Series named minutes where every value strictly above that percentile is replaced by the percentile value itself, while values at or below it are left unchanged. Every returned value is rounded to 2 decimal places, and entries follow the original row order.
constraints: The cap is readings['minutes'].quantile(0.9) computed over ALL rows (pandas default linear interpolation)
Values strictly above the cap become the cap; values at or below the cap stay as they were
All returned values rounded to 2 decimal places
Return a Series named 'minutes', one entry per input row, in the original row order

examples.returns: Series named 'minutes': the same 11 values but 90.0 is replaced by 16.3
examples.why: with 11 values the 90th percentile lands exactly on the 10th smallest (16.3), so the 90.0 spike is capped at 16.3

examples.returns: Series named 'minutes' where 15.0 becomes 14.0, all else unchanged
examples.why: the 90th percentile is 14.0, and only the single value above it (15.0) gets pulled down

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def cap_outliers(readings):
    """Return the minutes column with values above the 90th
    percentile replaced by that percentile.

    Series named 'minutes', original row order, all values
    rounded to 2 decimal places.
    """
    pass

tests.label: two spikes above an interpolated cap

hints: The threshold is not a number you are given — it is a statistic of the data. What single pandas call turns a column into 'the value below which 90% of the rows sit'?
Compute cap = readings['minutes'].quantile(0.9). Then you need 'replace every value above cap with cap, keep the rest' — there is a one-call method that does exactly this one-sided replacement.
cap = readings['minutes'].quantile(0.9); return readings['minutes'].clip(upper=cap).round(2). clip keeps values at or below the cap untouched and pulls larger ones down to it.
exercise.reasoning: Capping is a data-dependent rule: the threshold only exists once you have seen all the rows, which is why .quantile(0.9) must run on the whole column before any per-row decision. After that, the operation is the one-sided minimum min(value, cap) — precisely what .clip(upper=cap) computes for every row at once, leaving values at or below the cap untouched. Two determinism details make the answer checkable: pandas' percentile interpolation is fixed (linear), so the cap is reproducible; and rounding to 2 decimals pins the float noise that quantile interpolation can introduce.
